S7 teams Teams Counters Supreme League Guild Duel Heroes Caveats

Season 7 PvP report

Team groups, counters and drafting advice for Supreme League and Guild Duel.

Everything here, including the written insights, was produced by an automated analysis of saved tournament results and hero skill descriptions. No person wrote it, and no replays were reviewed, so explanations of wins and losses have not been checked against what happened during a battle, such as targeting or ability timing. The records primarily reflect top-spending players at the top end of the meta, with heavily upgraded rosters. The interpretations can be wrong, and results may differ with fewer upgrades. More about the data's limits.

A dotted-underlined record or count opens examples; a match or map link opens that match. This version leaves out player names.

Data as of 2026-09-19 · records created 2026-07-08 to 2026-09-19

1 · Team groups #

A team group contains related five-hero lineups that share heroes. Its name identifies the core, not a fixed team of five. heroes appear most often; heroes vary between lineups. Icon percentages show how often each hero appears. Every hero meeting the core or flex threshold is shown. Groups are sorted by strength tier, then by appearances. Strength estimates performance against an average team with equal upgrades, accounting for the opponents faced and recorded upgrade gaps. The full ratings include the unadjusted comparison.

excludes ties. shows how often the most popular artifact is equipped. The 95% interval below the win rate shows uncertainty from the number of games recorded; a wider range means a less precise estimate. It does not account for differences in players, upgrades or matches where players must reuse the same teams.

Insights

Place Gwyneth behind Gunnar and include Dunlingr high confidence

Gwyneth stands directly behind Gunnar on 448 of 454 boards fielding both. Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu is with Dunlingr and without him.

What to do Keep Gwyneth behind Gunnar and prioritize Dunlingr when the opponent may use Saida/Contess/Twins or Thador/Solise.

Gunnar gives the ally directly behind him extra range, attack and steadfast. That placement is part of the skill, so keep her behind him when changing the formation. Dunlingr adds a block on enemy ultimates at battle start: his Bell has one mode chosen before battle, and players usually use Spellbind. Gwyneth relies on normal attacks while many opposing teams need their first ultimates.

With Dunlingr, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu is against Saida/Contess/Twins and against Thador/Solise. Different players and opponents can affect those records, but his ultimate block gives a reason to favor this version against teams that need early casts.

Alna/Syph/Mehira needs the Winter Warrior buff on Sylphira and a path to the enemy medium confidence

Alna/Syph/Mehira is with Zandrok in Supreme League, against without him; the Guild Duel records are and .

What to do Place Sylphira so she receives Winter Warrior. Favor Zandrok where his Haste buff and wall destruction help the team reach the enemy.

Alna slows her own allies as well as the enemy. Her Winter Warrior escapes the Haste reduction and gains max HP: the closest ally in her diagonal row, ties to the frontmost unit. Across 471 Alna boards, Sylphira receives it 294 times, going 169–124 with a tie. The thirteen boards with nobody in the row went 3–10.

Zandrok helps the rest of the melee team with opening Haste and max HP, and his charge destroys breakable walls. That clears a route to the enemy and can remove a wall placed by Kulu. Permanent blocks remain. A battle-start charm from Mehira can interrupt his roar, so when both teams use Alna, check whether Mehira can interrupt Zandrok at battle start.

Evie/Orion benefits from Rolan but struggles when enemies stop its ultimates medium confidence

Evie/Orion is alongside Rolan, against without him.

What to do Use allies that cast ultimates frequently and keep Orion and Perseus safe so they can deal damage. Adding Rolan does not make the team reliable against Contess or Dunlingr.

Rolan supplies temporary buffs for Orion and benefits from frequent allied ultimates. Those casts also protect Evie: each ally ultimate lowers her Detection meter, keeping her concealed longer. Contess and Saida interfere with the casting that makes this work, while Dunlingr can prevent the opening ultimates. Orion is 20–52 with two ties against boards containing Contess, and 11–37 against boards containing Dunlingr. The Rolan split supports the build, but it does not turn its bad matchups into favorable ones.

Check the format before adding Rolan to Saida/Contess/Twins medium confidence

The Rolan version is in Supreme League but in Guild Duel.

What to do Practice the Rolan build, but place it where it is less likely to face Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu and check its Guild Duel evidence separately.

Saida/Contess/Twins punishes enemy ultimate casts while supplying its own healing and Energy. Rolan can support that team, but its strong Supreme League record does not establish the same advantage in Guild Duel. Check which opposing teams it would face and whether another team in your set needs Rolan more.

Rolan and the twins: choose supporting heroes your other teams can spare medium confidence

Rolan/Twins boards vary their supporting heroes, and the usual ones are also needed by other main teams.

What to do Check the full roster before using its record, and reserve the shared heroes before choosing the other teams.

Sylphira is on 67% of its boards, Taichi & Agumon on 49%, Contess and Mehira on 46% each, and Athalia on 26%. A Sylphira version competes directly with Alna/Syph/Mehira for heroes; a Contess version competes with Saida/Contess/Twins. Choose the version as part of your full set.

In Supreme League the boards with Contess are , against without her; the boards with Sylphira are , against without her. Different players and opponents sit behind those splits, and the counter records pool every version, so check which supporting heroes the recorded wins used before copying one.

Thador/Solise struggles against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu even with the usual formation medium confidence

Himmel’s party benefit depends on keeping Frieren, Thador and Solise adjacent, but that formation still needs a favorable opponent.

What to do Keep Himmel’s party members adjacent. Avoid placing Thador/Solise where it may face Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, even if your heroes have more upgrades.

Across boards fielding all four, the party is formed on 101 boards at 50–51; the six boards that break it are 0–6. That small comparison supports keeping the party together when practicing. Lily May can interrupt an early opposing ultimate, but cannot stop Gwyneth’s normal attacks. See the counter results before assigning this team to an opponent.

How team groups and common variations are defined

Teams are grouped by shared heroes. A hero on 80% or more of a group's boards counts as core; 15% to below 80% counts as flex. Every qualifying hero is shown, in order of usage, with no limit on the number of icons. These shares count recorded appearances, including ties and matches where players must reuse the same teams; they do not measure strength or independent draft choices. Rarer picks stay in the linked recorded teams, but are omitted from the core and flex lists. Artifacts do not determine the groups.

For common variations, we first find heroes often used together, then count only teams containing every listed hero. A row needs at least eight matching appearances in the team group. +1 flex means one other hero completes the team; expanding a row shows the actual heroes or combinations filling those slots. Rows can overlap, so their counts cannot be added together. Other recorded lineups keeps every exact team outside those rows, including rare picks and losing teams.

These cutoffs are analysis choices, not game rules. Broader or narrower groups can change a group's record. Each profile includes the results for its common variations, so you can compare recorded teams without listing every small variation as a separate group.

Flex comparisons can also differ in players, upgrades and opponents. A better record with a hero is worth testing, but does not prove that hero caused the improvement.

How the evidence labels work

Limited evidence means fewer than 30 games with a winner, 10 team selections or 5 players. Concentrated sample means one player contributes at least 35% of appearances, or the two most frequent players contribute at least 60%.

Promising flags a win rate of at least 60% with limited evidence. Poor results so far flags a win rate of 40% or less. These are reading aids, not statistical confidence tests or changes to the tiers. A winning record may depend on opponents or upgrades; a losing record can still include a useful counter.

The evidence in each profile shows the record without one most frequent player and at similar upgrades. When SL rules require the same teams for several matches, they count as one team selection per player and map. Separate selections can still share a strategy. Guild membership is not recorded, so these checks cannot identify teams copied within a guild. No team group is excluded for having a losing record.

How strength is measured, including upgrade differences

The model estimates a rating for each team group from its results against the other groups. A team rated r is expected to beat one rated s about r/(r+s) of the time. An average team is rated 1.00. These ratings compare teams with equal upgrades. This gives the expected win rate against an average team shown above.

The rating range in the table below comes from 3,000 repeated samples of 171 groups of related matches. Every match stays together. Matches where a player was required to reuse the same five teams also stay in one group. Each sample refits both team strength and the upgrade effect. Tier 1 requires the entire range to imply a win rate above 55% against an average team at equal upgrades (a rating above 1.22). Tier 3 means the entire rating range is below 1.00; all other teams are Tier 2. The tiers compare the recorded teams with each other: a Tier 3 team is still one that players field, rated below the others in this data rather than below every possible team. The same tiers group the teams in the counter ladder. This rating range is different from the observed win-rate interval in the main table. The same players can still recur in different stages, so these intervals do not remove every source of dependence.

The adjusted rating accounts for upgrades. A team can win partly because its heroes have more paragon or EX refinement than the opponent. The adjusted rating includes those differences when estimating team strength.

Both upgrades use one scale, Rivalry points. A paragon level is 4.5 points, the Inspiration/Intimidation it grants (each net point moves healing, shield value, extra Energy gains and buff effects by 1%). A refinement level is 0.9 points, its stat gains measured against a paragon level's, and the skill effect unlocked at R2 and the Rivalry-mode stats added at R4 are 2.1 points each, so a fully refined hero is worth 7.7 points against an unrefined one, about 1.7 paragon levels. The equal-upgrade rating uses each game's combined upgrade gap. The model estimates the effect of that gap, multiplying the advantaged side's odds by ×1.05 per net point (×1.24 for one paragon level on one hero, ×1.44 for one fully refined hero, ×1.53 for a 9-point gap), estimated from the 749 decided games where the sides were not equal. These are changes in odds, not percentage-point increases in win rate.

Players with more upgrades also tend to have better results. The model cannot fully separate their skill from their upgrades. A lower adjusted rating suggests that upgrade advantages explain part of the raw record. A higher one suggests the team performed well despite having fewer upgrades.

Tiers use the equal-upgrade rating and its resampled interval. The unadjusted rating remains a comparison. Near level is the team's record in games where the combined upgrade gap was below 4.5 points, equivalent to one paragon level on one hero. The recorded games do not show a winning advantage for gaps that small.

Is refinement weighted right? The same model run with paragon and refinement weighted separately prefers a refinement point at 1.21 of a paragon point, from the 481 decided games that carried a refinement gap. That is a point estimate, with no interval for the exchange rate. Allowing separate effects improves the log-likelihood, a measure of fit to these recorded outcomes, by 0.19. That is little improvement, so these results do not give a strong reason to change the agreed scale. Both fits still mix upgrade effects with differences between players and their teams.

How to read the formation diagrams and their percentages

Each diagram shows the group's usual lineup as it was actually placed on a ground in the Supreme League rotation. The team is the five-hero line-up the group fielded most often on those grounds, with each line-up's uses weighted by how common its heroes are within the group (the Core and Flex percentages multiplied together), so the board shows the popular flex picks rather than a placement one player repeated with an unusual pick. Guild Duel games count when they were played on a ground that is also a Supreme League map (GD-Map1 and GD-Map2 are); Guild Duel's other grounds are left out, because Guild Duel is played far more often and would otherwise decide the board. The ground shown is the one where that team was placed the same way most often, named by its Supreme League map position, and the caption counts uses of that exact placement. It is an example of placement, not a recommendation to choose that map. A team group never recorded on a Supreme League ground is drawn from all of its boards. Enemy-side formations are mirrored so both sides can be compared.

Placed here is how often a unit used that tile; on N% of boards is how often it appeared. Both refer to the team group on the diagram's map. The core and flex percentages in the main table instead cover all maps.

The phantimal is summoned automatically from the team's factions. You choose its tile, which can affect targeting and artifact effects, but do not select it independently of the heroes.

One-off line-ups #

These teams fall outside the named team groups; some have been played more than once.

Line-ups outside the named groups that beat an established team rated average or better. Each row is one exact five-hero build. Treat a row as a lead worth testing, not a proven answer. Most have a handful of games. Pay particular attention to wins with similar or fewer upgrades. Select a record to see sample games the line-up played against named teams, or a map name to see that whole match.

Which counters have statistical support? #

A losing record alone does not establish a counter. The team may struggle against many opponents or on that particular map. The test compares its record against this opponent with its record against everyone else on the same maps, then combines those comparisons. Each game's upgrade gap also affects the expected outcome: losing while far behind on paragon and refinement is less evidence of a counter, and winning from behind is more. Games with teams from the same group on both sides are excluded. A map contributes no comparison if the team faced only one opponent there.

All win rates below are for the team in the first column; wins–losses appear in parentheses.

Near level keeps only games with an upgrade gap below 4.5 points, combining paragon and refinement. It helps show whether the losing record also appears when upgrades are similar. Player skill and team differences can still affect it. Win-rate gap is the difference between the two win rates, in percentage points.

The p-value describes how unusual a result this extreme would be if there were no special matchup effect after accounting for maps and upgrade gaps. Smaller values provide stronger evidence under the test's assumptions. It is not the probability that a counter is false.

How reliable are these counters?

Testing many matchups can produce chance findings. 29 pairs of team groups had enough games to test in both directions (58 tests). The counter table labels results with p-values below 0.05 as supported. A stricter threshold divides 0.05 by the number of tests to reduce the chance of finding a counter just because many comparisons were made. The counter insights identify which matchups meet that threshold.

Repeated games are not independent examples. The same players can appear many times, sometimes because SL rules require them to reuse the same teams for several matches. Each matchup's details include a recount by whole match, the number of player pairs, and a breakdown when one player accounts for a large share of the games. Those checks help show how much the result depends on repeated games or particular players; they do not remove those effects.

The opponents still matter. A team's record against everyone else includes one-off line-ups, which can make it look stronger. Comparing results on the same maps and pricing upgrade gaps does not remove differences in player skill or the exact teams used. The fitted upgrade effect can also include differences between players; these records do not separate those effects.

The upgrade effect is estimated. The counter test treats that fitted value as fixed. Its p-values do not include uncertainty in the upgrade estimate, and repeated appearances by the same players and teams also limit their precision. Statistical support is a reason to investigate a matchup, not a calibrated chance of winning it.

The team grouping rules can also affect the result. Every supported counter was also checked with broader and narrower groups.

Insights

Six counters have stronger statistical evidence high confidence

Alna/Syph/Mehira over Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Saida/Contess/Twins, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Evie/Orion, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Thador/Solise, Evie/Orion over Zorya/Athalia/Pandora and Zorya/Athalia/Pandora over Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu meet the stricter threshold used for the 58 comparisons. Evie/Orion over Alna/Syph/Mehira, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu over Rolan/Twins, Saida/Contess/Twins over Evie/Orion and Rolan/Twins over Evie/Orion clear the ordinary 0.05 line but not the stricter one. The test counts each game by its upgrade gap, so a win taken while behind on upgrades counts for more than one taken with an edge.

What to do Use these counters when choosing teams for a likely matchup. Rolan/Twins still needs more games against Evie/Orion with similar upgrades.

The counter table gives the records and near-level comparisons. Zorya/Athalia/Pandora over Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu meets the stricter threshold at the fitted upgrade effect, but only the ordinary threshold at the lower end of the effect's resampled interval. Evie/Orion against Zorya/Athalia/Pandora is , with of those games near level. Rolan/Twins against Evie/Orion is but only with similar upgrades, so its strong overall result still needs particular care.

The confirmed mechanics support these directions. Alna slows the Gunnar pair while Sylphira attacks its clustered backline; Zandrok helps the melee team reach it. Dunlingr prevents the opening casts Saida/Contess/Twins and Thador/Solise need, and his block also starves Evie’s team of the ultimates that keep her hidden while Gwyneth’s normal attacks are unaffected: Orion is 11–37 against boards with Dunlingr and 14–38 against boards with Gwyneth. Contess punishes casts and Saida drains Energy, undermining the allied ultimates that keep Evie concealed. Zorya does nothing until her Energy fills, so a team that attacks early can remove her support pieces before she wakes. A statistical label still describes recorded evidence, not a guaranteed result.

Evidence Threshold after accounting for all comparisons: 0.05 / 58 = 0.00086

Evie/Orion leads against Alna/Syph/Mehira, but the support is still limited medium confidence

Evie/Orion is against Alna/Syph/Mehira and with similar upgrades; the comparison accounting for maps and upgrades clears the 0.05 line but not the stricter threshold.

What to do Use Evie as a candidate against Alna, and compare it with a practiced mirror rather than assuming a proven counter exists.

Evie can begin inside the enemy half while invincible, which gives a reason to test the pairing. The recorded lead remains too uncertain to treat it as a dependable answer. Compare the exact formation with a practiced mirror (see the mirror insight), and check the map and upgrade differences.

Zorya/Athalia/Pandora beats Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu while behind on upgrades, but struggles badly against other teams low confidence

Zorya/Athalia/Pandora is against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, and in the games where it was behind on upgrades, so the test that counts each game by its upgrade gap strongly supports the counter. With similar upgrades it is only , so the evidence rests on games where the Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu side had more upgrades.

What to do Use Zorya only for a specific expected matchup with a team you have practiced. Check whether the opponent can respond with Evie/Orion or Saida/Contess/Twins.

Its Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu results also differ by map: 5–3 on SL map 1, 6–5 on SL map 2 and 3–1 across the current SL maps 3 and 4, but 2–6 on SL map 5. Practice the intended formation and arena before using it as an alternative to Alna/Syph/Mehira.

It is against Evie/Orion and against Saida/Contess/Twins. Before choosing Zorya against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu, check whether the set can still win if the opponent changes the order and Zorya faces one of those teams.

5 · Heroes #

Rolan: skills and placement #

The three most-used tiles on each current SL map, as a share of Rolan's appearances there. Enemy-side positions are mirrored.

How his skills work
A Celestial support built around a team Morale meter. Battle starts at 20% Morale (more when the team uses heroes from one faction, most of all Lightbearers or Celestials, who also take 50% less damage for 8s); every 20% Morale gives every ally ATK worth 10% of Rolan's; every ally ultimate adds 10% (Elijah & Lailah's ultimate counts twice), each kill adds 10%, each death costs 10%, and if Rolan dies the meter is wiped.
At 60% Morale
His blessing on the two highest-damage allies (control-immune for 10s, +ATK) adds 50 Haste, and his heal also stuns the densest enemy cluster for 3s.
At 100% Morale
A radiant ward: each ally ultimate spawns a clone that casts it again, Morale can no longer drop while he lives, and allies inside are immune to stat reductions.
Ultimate
Cleanses allies, equalizes their HP percentages, grants +150% max HP decaying over 12s and a large heal, plus 15% Morale.

Skills from the app's text for Rolan; numbers rounded. The insights below explain how these skills affect team choices.

Placement advice

Placing Rolan farther back may help, but does not guarantee a win medium confidence

Back-row placements have winning records, but the direct comparison between teams that both used Rolan is too close to establish that farther back is better.

What to do Place Rolan where his allies can protect him from the enemy’s opening attacks. The back corner is not always safest.

His death removes Morale, so protection matters. The two Rolans can also have different teammates. A corner can expose him to enemies that target the rearmost hero; check those skills and his allies’ protection before moving him farther back.

Evidence Rows from center: 4 rows 82–38–1t; 3 rows 102–40–1t; 2 rows 38–26; 1 row 1–2; center row 11–12 · Both teams used Rolan: Rolan farther back won 14 of 26

A mirror needs a practiced build and an upgrade check medium confidence

The player with the higher overall win rate won 102 of 147 decided mirrors within named team groups. Where a mirror had an upgrade gap of at least one level, the advantaged side went 63–16 with three ties.

What to do Practice the full formation and check investment before choosing a mirror as the answer.

Using the same team group as the opponent is an option when no counter is established, but those observations do not make it an automatic win for the stronger player. Build differences, placement and battle-start interactions remain. Private 1v1 tests can help compare a flex change under otherwise similar conditions; they do not replace tournament evidence or establish the set’s minimum win chance.

Gwyneth: skills, placement and the best version of her team #

The three most-used tiles on each current SL map, as a share of Gwyneth's appearances there. Enemy-side positions are mirrored.

How her skills work
A Lightbearer marksman whose damage comes from her normal attacks, which run in a cycle of three. The second arrow deals heavy fire damage and burns the target, lowering its Vitality; the third silences the target for 1s and splashes lightning over every enemy within 2 tiles, stunning them briefly. With her Exclusive Equipment the first arrow carries both effects and all her normal attacks deal 20–30% more; at its third level that arrow also strikes for 10% of the target's max HP and ignores most of its physical defense.
Ultimate
Rains arrows over the tile with the most enemies and every tile within 2 of it, immobilizing them for 2s. Her charged normal attack also hits harder the more attack speed and Haste she has.
Distance
Hero Focus gives her attack speed during battle and more of it when no enemy has been within 1 tile of her for 3s; her Enhance Force awakening then shortens the gap between her normal attacks by 40% under the same condition. Everything in her kit rewards standing where enemies cannot reach her quickly, and Gunnar's bonus range to the ally directly behind him lets her hit from there.

Gwyneth, Gunnar, Kulu and Dunlingr with Aliceth is the best-supported version high confidence

What to do Start from Gwyneth, Gunnar, Kulu, Dunlingr and Aliceth. Use Cyran as the fifth hero when Aliceth is needed elsewhere, and favor Dunlingr against teams that need early ultimates.

Evidence Line-ups compared: the 12 most-used exact line-ups, out of 67 recorded

Keep Gwyneth in the back two rows, directly behind Gunnar high confidence

Inside Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu she is in the back two rows and one row further forward.

What to do Place Gunnar in the third row from the center line or deeper, with Gwyneth directly behind him. Bringing her forward to reach a target costs the attack speed her kit is built on.

Her attack speed bonus from Hero Focus and the 40% faster attacks from her awakening both need 3s without an enemy within 1 tile of her, so a tile that enemies reach late keeps her firing at full speed. Gunnar gives the ally directly behind him extra range, attack and steadfast, which is why she stands there on almost every board. When you move the pair, move them together.

Evie: where to start her on each Supreme League map #

How her skills work
When the battle starts, Intel Chase teleports Evie to the tile on the enemy half that mirrors her own and hides her there, invincible. She immediately gathers intel on every enemy hero within 1 tile of where she lands, then on the rest one at a time from nearest to farthest, 4.5s each, gaining 150 Energy per hero. Her Detection meter fills at 120 a second and every ally ultimate takes 500 off it; at 1000 she is revealed where she stands and loses her invincibility. Once every enemy is investigated she teleports back to her own tile.
Why the landing tile matters
Without ally ultimates she has about 8s hidden. Enemies next to her landing tile are investigated together in the first 4.5s; each enemy farther away costs another 4.5s. Every investigated hero loses 20% Magic DEF for the battle, and investigating all of them while hidden takes another 25% off every enemy, makes them deal 25–35% less damage through her Exclusive Equipment, and with her awakening adds a second healing quill. Landing next to the enemy line is how she finishes in time.
Active skills
Her ultimate interrogates the enemy with the most damage dealt, immobilizing it for 6–8s and silencing it if already investigated; Pointed Proof dashes to the nearest enemy for two dagger strikes; Foretold Favor's quill heals and buffs the ally dealing the most damage.

Skills from the app's text for Evie; numbers rounded. The landing tile is the point-symmetric tile on the enemy half, the same mapping this report uses to mirror enemy positions.

Amber tiles are her three most-used starts on each map, with her record from each. The blue tile is the start whose landing tile has had the most enemy heroes next to it, averaged over every enemy deployment recorded on that map, whatever team Evie's side played; it is drawn as a blue border when it is also one of her starts. The opponent's team changes where enemies stand, so treat the blue tile as the usual case, not a rule.

Placement advice

Start Evie where her landing tile touches the enemy line medium confidence

On SL maps 1 to 3 the usual start, tile 4, lands next to 2.7, 2.9 and 3.2 enemies on average. On map 5 the usual start, tile 3, lands next to only 1.5; tile 7 would touch 2.8.

What to do On maps 1, 2 and 3 keep her on tile 4, or on tile 7 on maps 1 and 2 when the formation allows it. On map 4 prefer tile 4 to tile 2, and on map 5 test tile 7 instead of tile 3.

She investigates every enemy within 1 tile of her landing spot at once and the rest one at a time, 4.5s each, with about 8s hidden unless allies cast ultimates. Landing next to three enemies leaves two more to investigate, so two ally ultimates finish the job; landing next to one leaves four, which no realistic number of casts covers before she is revealed on the enemy side.

On map 4 the two common starts differ the same way: tile 2 lands next to 1.1 enemies and tile 4 next to 2.8. The landing tile is the point-symmetric tile on the enemy half, and where enemies stand depends on their team, so count the enemies her landing tile will touch against the opponent’s usual formation before trusting the average.

Evidence Start whose landing tile touches the most enemies: map 1 tile 7 (2.9); map 2 tile 7 (3.2); map 3 tile 4 (3.1); map 4 tile 4 (3.0); map 5 tile 7 (2.8), averaged over every recorded enemy deployment on the arena

Her results by start tile do not separate the tiles yet low confidence

Tile 4 is on map 1, on map 2 and on map 3. The second choices, tile 5 on maps 1 and 2 ( and ) and tile 6 on map 3 (), have better records from smaller samples that land next to fewer enemies.

What to do Choose the tile by the enemies it will touch, then check that map’s records in the table above.

Those records mix players, opponents, upgrades and the rest of her team, and the smaller samples are too few to show that the second choices are better tiles. On map 4, tile 2 is despite landing far from the enemy, and the three boards that started her on the forward tile 14 all won: landing away from everyone has not cost games there, although it leaves her investigations slow. Treat the adjacency numbers as the reason to pick a tile and the records as a check that the choice has not gone wrong.

Evidence Map 4 forward tile 14: 3 boards, 3–0, landing next to no enemy

Solid chips mean core, outlined chips mean flex. Presence is the share of the 1078 games they appear in, and since both sides can field the same hero the ceiling is 200%. Lift is their win rate minus the average win rate of the players who brought them, a rough way to tell a strong hero from a hero that strong players like.

6 · Caveats #

These results include matches from multiple contributors and leagues, analyzed without replays. Many matchups have few games. Player skill, hero upgrades and the rules used to group similar teams can affect the results. Ties are excluded from win rates. Read these limits before relying on a particular number.

The caveats in full

Players and teams are represented unevenly. A team's results can depend on who used it, their opponents and their upgrades. Games where a player must reuse the same teams are related results, not separate tests of a new team choice. Check the matchup's player and format breakdowns before applying its overall record to another situation.

Tied maps are left out of win rates. The game gives a tied battle to one player, the defending side, and the match lists color a tied map for that player. Winning a map on a tie does not show that the team won the battle, so every win rate leaves ties out.

Missing upgrade levels use match-wide rules. Paragon levels are recorded in 944 games and refinement levels in 549. If a match has no recorded levels for one upgrade type, every hero is treated as level 4 for that type. If any levels are recorded, a hero without a row is level 0.

The strength section explains the upgrade scale and adjusted ratings, and holds each team's record with the upgrade advantage, behind it and near level.
